title: Thanksgiving Groceries Up 11%, Turkey 26% in National Count - Uprise RI
text:
Thanksgiving Groceries Up 11%, Turkey 26% in National Count Skip to main content     Newsletter Advertise Donate Toggle theme Account Select Town Rhode Island's Local News Leader News Local Features BillBuddy Our Reporting Games Contact Consumer Watch · November 18, 2026 · 4 min read National Count Puts Thanksgiving Groceries Up 11%, Turkey Up 26%
 A national analysis by Groundwork Collaborative and The Century Foundation puts a 26-item Thanksgiving list up 11%, with a 15-pound turkey up 26%. Federal grocery data and a PwC forecast show smaller increases.
 Kaelen Valeborn Consumer Watch Why This Matters Rhode Islanders planning a holiday meal face a turkey priced 26% higher in a national count, though federal grocery inflation ran at 1.8%. Most stores in the state must close on Thanksgiving Day, November 26.
 A 15-pound frozen turkey rings up at $19.65 in a new national holiday grocery tally, up from $15.60 a year earlier. That 26% increase is the centerpiece of an analysis that puts the overall Thanksgiving list up 11%.
 The figures come from Groundwork Collaborative and The Century Foundation , two policy groups that published the analysis Tuesday. Their table prices 26 holiday items using NielsenIQ data and totals them at $137.12, against $123.52 for the earlier period. NielsenIQ, the market research firm that supplied the prices, states on the table that it had no role in the analysis or its conclusions.
 The groups tie the increases to the war with Iran and the Trump administration's trade and tariff policy.
 What the 11% is made of
 The total adds one price for each item on the list, with quantities set by each label: "1 can," "2 cans," "15lbs." It is a shopping list priced item by item, not a weighted measure of what a particular household spends on its meal.
 That matters most when you look down the list, because the items did not move together. Elbow macaroni rose 40.2%. Green beans rose 36.7%. Cream of mushroom soup, pecans and foil each climbed about 22%.
 Then there is the other end of the table. Cranberry sauce rose 1.7%. Butternut squash rose 1.8%. Rolls rose 2.2%, and spiral ham 2.9%.
 A family that skips the green bean casserole and leans on ham will feel a different holiday than one built around a big bird and a pan of mac and cheese. The turkey line alone, at $4.05 more, carries a large share of the list's increase.
 One detail in the source table bears on the phrase "this year": the table's title compares 2026 with 2025, while its footnote says the NielsenIQ data covers one-week periods ending Oct. 31, 2024, and Oct. 30, 2025.
 Local sponsor Kyle Moore, the Century Foundation's chief economist, told Scripps News the increase continues a trend of inflation across goods. Emily DiVito, Groundwork's senior advisor for economic policy, described it to the outlet as the start of an expensive holiday season.
 What the federal numbers show
 The official grocery yardstick tells a milder story, and it measures something different. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Oct. 14 that its food-at-home index, which tracks grocery prices broadly rather than a holiday list, rose 1.8% over the 12 months ending in September. Food overall rose 2.5%. Prices for everything, the headline consumer price index, rose 3.7%, with gasoline up 34.2% over the same stretch.
 The agency's newer numbers are thinner. In its Nov. 10 release, BLS said it cannot publish 12-month changes for October because October 2025 data were not collected during a lapse in federal appropriations. Nationally, food at home rose 0.4% from September to October, seasonally adjusted.
 A private forecast lands closer to the federal figure than to 11%. Ali Furman, consumer markets industry leader at PwC, told ABC7 New York on Oct. 16 that a Thanksgiving was expected to cost about $90, compared with $88 last year.
 Those are three different tools: a 26-item holiday list, an index of everything people buy at the grocery store, and a meal forecast. They answer different questions, and none of them is wrong for disagreeing with the others.
 The Rhode Island picture
 The holiday table's prices are national. The closest official read for Rhode Island comes from the BLS Northeast region, which includes the state. There, food at home rose 0.6% from September to October. Northeast prices for all items were up 4.2% over the 12 months ending in September, higher than the national 3.7%.
 Timing is the other local factor. Under Rhode Island General Laws § 5-23-2 , retail stores may not open on Thanksgiving Day, which falls on November 26 this year, apart from listed exceptions. One exception covers food retailers with fewer than six employees per shift at any one location. The law was most recently amended in 2025, with the change taking effect Jan. 1, 2026.
 Next price checks
 More numbers are coming before the holiday. The American Farm Bureau Federation, which has priced a fixed classic Thanksgiving dinner for 10 since 1986, is slated to release its 2026 survey Wednesday, according to the federation's June 24 release. Its 2025 survey put that dinner at $55.18, the third straight annual decline. Questions about the survey go to Mike Tomko, the federation's director of communications, at (202) 406-3642 or [email protected] .
 Readers can examine the Groundwork and Century Foundation table, item by item, on Groundwork's site. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes its November price data on Dec. 10 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern.
